```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.align = "center",
                      dpi = 200, fig.retina = 2, dev = "ragg_png", dev.args = list(bg = "white"),
                      fig.width = 6, fig.height = 6,
                      calor.autosize = TRUE)
# Size each figure to its plot: ggcalor plots have a natural size in mm.
knitr::opts_hooks$set(calor.autosize = function(options) {
  if (!isTRUE(options$calor.autosize) || !isTRUE(options$eval)) return(options)
  env <- new.env(parent = knitr::knit_global())
  seed <- get0(".Random.seed", envir = globalenv(), inherits = FALSE)
  res <- try(suppressMessages(eval(parse(text = options$code), envir = env)), silent = TRUE)
  if (!is.null(seed)) assign(".Random.seed", seed, envir = globalenv())
  if (inherits(res, "ggplot")) {
    sz <- try(ggcalor::calor_size(res) / 25.4 + 0.15, silent = TRUE)
    if (!inherits(sz, "try-error") && all(sz > 1)) {
      options$fig.width <- sz[1]; options$fig.height <- sz[2]
      options$out.width <- paste0(round(sz[1] * 96), "px")
    }
  }
  options
})
```

Each recipe below is one complete example on real data, with a short note on
what the verbs do and why the plot is built that way. Copy the code, swap in
your own matrix, and adjust.

```{r setup}
library(ggcalor)
```

## Clustered heatmap with annotations

The `dune` data from vegan records the cover (on a 1–9 scale) of 30 plant
species in 20 Dutch meadows, along with how each meadow is managed and how wet
it is. A clustered heatmap shows which species occur together and which sites
are alike.

```{r dune}
data(dune, dune.env, package = "vegan")
sites <- data.frame(management = dune.env$Management, moisture = dune.env$Moisture,
                    row.names = rownames(dune))
levels(sites$management) <- c("biological", "hobby", "nature reserve", "standard")

ggcalor(t(dune), cell_size = 4.2) +
  calor_dendro(rows = TRUE, cols = TRUE, k = 3, highlight = TRUE) +
  calor_split(cols = 3) +
  calor_anno(top = sites) +
  calor_margin(right = "mean") +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Greens", direction = 1) +
  labs(fill = "cover")
```

`calor_dendro()` clusters both axes and draws the trees. With `k = 3` it cuts
each tree into three groups, and `highlight = TRUE` shades them.
`calor_split(cols = 3)` then separates the three column groups with a gap;
cells stay square and each slice keeps its own subtree.

`calor_anno()` takes a data frame whose row names match the columns. Each
column becomes one track. Unordered factors get distinct qualitative colours,
and ordered factors such as `moisture` get a light-to-dark sequence.
`calor_margin(right = "mean")` adds a bar of each species' mean cover.

The final order is available for reuse, for example to order a table the same
way:

```{r order}
p <- ggcalor(t(dune)) + calor_dendro(rows = TRUE, cols = TRUE)
str(calor_order_of(p))
```

## Your own plots beside the heatmap

`calor_panel()` attaches any ggplot to a side of the heatmap. Map the row
names to `y` (for a left or right panel) or the column names to `x` (for a
top or bottom panel) and write the rest as ordinary ggplot2 code: geoms,
scales, themes and labels are kept as you wrote them. ggcalor only lines the
names up with the cells, after clustering, ordering and splitting.

```{r panel}
m <- t(dune)
species <- data.frame(species = rownames(m), mean = rowMeans(m),
                      se = apply(m, 1, sd) / sqrt(ncol(m)))
bars <- ggplot(species, aes(mean, species)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#74A9CF", width = 0.7) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = mean - se, xmax = mean + se), width = 0.3, linewidth = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "mean cover \u00b1 se") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 8)

present <- data.frame(site = rep(colnames(m), each = nrow(m)), cover = as.vector(m))
present <- present[present$cover > 0, ]
boxes <- ggplot(present, aes(site, cover)) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.6, fill = "grey90", outlier.size = 0.4, linewidth = 0.3) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 8)

ggcalor(m, cell_size = 4.2) +
  calor_dendro(rows = TRUE, cols = TRUE) +
  calor_split(cols = 3) +
  calor_panel(bars, side = "right", size = 28) +
  calor_panel(boxes, side = "top", size = 18) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Greens", direction = 1) +
  labs(fill = "cover")
```

The boxplots follow the clustered site order, gaps included, and the bars
follow the species. Because the panels match by name, the order of rows in
your data frame does not matter. A legend in a panel (say, bars filled by
group) joins the heatmap's legends.

## Scaled columns, glyphs and brackets

When columns are measured in different units, scale them first.
`scale = "column"` z-scores every column, so each cell shows how far a car sits
from the average for that variable.

```{r cars}
vars <- c("cyl", "disp", "hp", "carb", "wt", "drat", "gear", "mpg", "qsec")
group <- rep(c("engine", "chassis", "performance"), c(4, 3, 2))
transmission <- ifelse(mtcars$am == 1, "manual", "automatic")

ggcalor(as.matrix(mtcars[, vars]), cell_size = 4, scale = "column") +
  calor_dendro(rows = TRUE, k = 2, highlight = TRUE) +
  calor_split(rows = 2) +
  calor_anno(left = list(transmission = transmission), type = "glyph") +
  calor_bracket(cols = group, side = "bottom", angle = 90, size = 14) +
  calor_legend("histogram") +
  labs(fill = "z-score")
```

`type = "glyph"` draws a categorical track as symbols rather than coloured
tiles. This keeps the colour for the heatmap itself. `calor_bracket()` labels
runs of adjacent columns. `calor_legend("histogram")` replaces the colour bar
with a histogram of all values painted in the fill scale, so the legend also
shows how the values are distributed.

## Oncoprint

A character matrix gets a discrete fill. `luad_alterations` has one row per
gene and one column per TCGA lung adenocarcinoma, with `NA` where a gene is
not altered. To keep the cells square at a readable width, we keep the ten
most often altered genes and the tumours altered in at least one of them.

```{r oncoprint}
alt_colours <- c(mutation = "#2E7D32", amplification = "#C62828",
                 `deep deletion` = "#1565C0", `mutation + amplification` = "#8E24AA")

n_altered <- rowSums(!is.na(luad_alterations))
m <- luad_alterations[order(n_altered, decreasing = TRUE)[1:10], ]
m <- m[, colSums(!is.na(m)) > 0]

ggcalor(m, cell_size = 2.6, cell_gap = 0.25, border = NA, labels = "rows") +
  calor_order(rows = "sum", cols = "memo") +
  calor_margin(right = "sum", top = "sum", size = 10) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = alt_colours, breaks = names(alt_colours), na.value = "grey93") +
  labs(fill = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

`calor_order(rows = "sum")` puts the most frequently altered genes on top.
`cols = "memo"` is the memo sort used by cBioPortal. It orders samples so
that those altered in the top gene come first, then the next gene, and so on,
which turns mutual exclusivity into a staircase. Giving `breaks` in
`scale_fill_manual()` keeps the empty cells (`NA`) painted with `na.value`
but out of the legend. `labels = "rows"` shows the gene names and hides the
sample IDs, which say nothing here.

## Correlation matrix

Order first, then mask. Here the variables are ordered by clustering on
`1 - r`, and `mask = upper.tri(cm)` hides the redundant upper triangle. A
transparent `na_fill` makes the masked cells disappear.

```{r correlation}
cm <- cor(mtcars)
o <- hclust(as.dist(1 - cm))$order
cm <- cm[o, o]

ggcalor(cm, cell_size = 8, mask = upper.tri(cm), cell_gap = 0.08, border = NA, na_fill = NA) +
  calor_text(digits = 2, size = 5.5) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "RdBu", limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(fill = "r")
```

Setting `limits = c(-1, 1)` centres the diverging palette on zero and keeps
the colour bar on the full range of a correlation.

## Calendar heatmaps

A month-by-year grid is a heatmap too. `AirPassengers` gives monthly airline
passengers (in thousands) from 1949 to 1960.

```{r calendar}
air <- matrix(AirPassengers, 12, dimnames = list(month.abb, 1949:1960))

ggcalor(air, cell_size = 7, cell_gap = 0.1, border = NA) +
  calor_text(digits = 0, size = 5) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Blues", direction = 1) +
  labs(fill = "passengers\n(thousands)")
```

Both the growth over the years (left to right) and the summer peak each year
(July and August) show up at once. `calor_radial()` bends the same grid into a
ring, with years running outwards from 1949 in the middle:

```{r calendar-ring}
ggcalor(t(air)[12:1, ], cell_size = 4, cell_gap = 0.1, border = NA) +
  calor_radial(inner.radius = 0.3, gap = 0.35, legend = "outside", label_size = 8) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Blues", direction = 1) +
  labs(fill = "passengers\n(thousands)")
```

## Ring of categories

Long data goes straight in through `rows`, `cols` and `value`, one row per
cell. `dvs_members` lists the months in which each of 130 countries gained
members of a society, with their dominant trait. `calor_radial()` places the
country names around the ring, the months in the gap, and the legend in the
hole. The country names are real; the memberships are simulated.

```{r ring}
ggcalor(dvs_members, rows = "month", cols = "country", value = "trait",
        cell_size = 2.4, border = "grey85", na_fill = "white") +
  calor_radial(inner.radius = 0.45) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Data = "#f2c200", Visualization = "#e03b3b",
                               Society = "#4a7bd0"), na.translate = FALSE) +
  labs(fill = NULL)
```

## Smooth surfaces

When rows and columns are positions on a regular grid, like the heights of
the Maunga Whau volcano in `volcano`, a smooth surface reads better than cells.
`smooth = "contour"` interpolates the matrix onto a finer grid, blurs it by
`smooth_sigma` cells, and draws filled contour bands at rounded break values.

```{r surface}
v <- t(volcano[seq(87, 1, -2), seq(1, 61, 2)])
dimnames(v) <- list(seq_len(nrow(v)), seq_len(ncol(v)))

ggcalor(v, cell_size = 2.4, smooth = "contour", smooth_sigma = 1, labels = "none") +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "mako") +
  labs(fill = "height (m)")
```

`smooth = "raster"` draws the same surface as a continuous image:

```{r surface-raster}
ggcalor(v, cell_size = 2.4, smooth = "raster", labels = "none") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "mako") +
  labs(fill = "height (m)")
```

## Hex cells

`cell_shape = "hex"` tiles the grid with hexagons, offsetting every other row.

```{r hex}
hx <- volcano[seq(1, 87, 5), seq(1, 61, 4)]
dimnames(hx) <- list(seq_len(nrow(hx)), seq_len(ncol(hx)))

ggcalor(hx, cell_shape = "hex", cell_size = 5, cell_gap = 0.06, labels = "none") +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Spectral") +
  labs(fill = "height (m)")
```

## Waffle charts

`ggwaffle()` draws counts as a grid of unit cells, one waffle per group. Here
each square is 1% of the penguins sampled on each island.

```{r waffle}
penguins <- as.data.frame(table(island = palmerpenguins::penguins$island,
                                species = palmerpenguins::penguins$species))
ggwaffle(penguins, "species", "Freq", by = "island", cell_size = 2.6)
```

## Interactive

With ggiraph installed, `calor_interactive()` adds tooltips to the cells and
categorical tracks, and hovering a cell highlights its whole row (or column,
with `data_id = "col"`). `calor_girafe()` renders the result as an HTML
widget.

```{r interactive, eval = FALSE}
p <- ggcalor(t(dune), cell_size = 4.2) +
  calor_dendro(rows = TRUE, cols = TRUE) +
  calor_anno(top = sites) +
  calor_interactive(data_id = "row")
calor_girafe(p)
```

## Saving

A ggcalor plot knows its own size: the cells, trees, tracks, labels and legend
add up to a fixed width and height in millimetres. `calor_size()` reports it,
and `calor_save()` passes it to `ggsave()`, so the file holds exactly the plot
you built with no squashed cells or empty borders.

```{r save, eval = FALSE}
calor_size(p)
calor_save(p, "dune.pdf")
calor_save(p, "dune.png", dpi = 300)
```
